heard: Early space scientists feared the moon was a deep, swallowing dust ocean. This theory suggested heavy landers would sink completely out of sight upon touchdown. In 1966, the Soviet Union's Luna 9 probe achieved the first soft landing. NASA's Surveyor one followed months later, resting solidly on the firm lunar surface. Robotic scoops excavated trenches, proving the regolith could easily support a crewed lander. But after sunset, Surveyor 7 captured a strange, unexpected glow along the horizon. Sunlight was scattering off razor-sharp dust grains, levitating miles above the airless ground. This grit is electrostatically charged as the moon passes through Earth's magnetic tail. The real lunar hazard was actually floating in the sky.
